title: Fukanzazengi Part 6
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: The talk emphasizes the importance of being present and aware in meditation practice, suggesting that simply showing up with an open mind is enough, rather than trying to achieve a specific state or skill. This approach is rooted in Dogen's text Phukan Zazengi, which challenges traditional notions of meditation as a skill to be learned and mastered. By embracing this mindset, individuals can cultivate a deeper understanding of their own nature and the true value of Zen practice lies not in its historical accuracy, but in its ability to convey a wordless, transcendent reality.

sentences.text: Well, it's possible that in a dharma talk we can say something encouraging or helpful, or some information that somebody can make use of to support their life.
That's possible, and so we prepare talks and try to think about what we're going to say.
But I was thinking about it a little while ago, and maybe the real virtue of a dharma talk is not the words, or what the speaker thinks is going to happen, so much as just an excuse to come together.
A reason to be together in a community, bringing forth our intention.
You may think you're just sitting there, but actually everyone who's here is in some way bringing forth their intention.
We don't always know what that is exactly, or we can't always verbalize what we mean by my intention.
But we showed up here.
Everywhere we show up, we're showing up for our life, and this is a particular way of showing up for our life.
There's some interest expressed just by our presence, and a great, powerful sense of mutual support, which you can really feel if you feel for it.
So thanks for that.
I thought tonight we would try to complete our exploration of Master Dogen's text about seated meditation called Fukanzazengi, the universal recommendation for Zazen, for seated meditation.
And during meditation, contrary to Dogen's instructions, I was thinking about a line earlier in the text.
This text is in the [unclear: "champ book"].
You can open it later when I start quoting lines, if you like.
Earlier in the text, some talks ago (this was the sixth talk on this little two page text), he says that Zazen is not learning meditation.
I mean, that's a different text.
*Zazen is not learning meditation.
It is simply the dharma gate of repose and bliss.*
*Zazen is not learning meditation.
It is simply the dharma gate of repose and bliss.*
A lot of his teachings seem to be designed to short-circuit our usual attitude.
We hope, in a wholesome and helpful way, for our life.
Of course we think Zazen is learning meditation.

We think of these things as skills, as things to take up that will help us, things we want to get better at, things we don't want to screw up on, things we want to live up to snuff on and do a good job.
We also hope for some result, some more peacefulness or calm from our meditation skill.
And it would also be nice to have some sort of internal or external markers to tell us that we're doing a good job.
We're also seeking validation, right, whenever we take up a new skill.
So Dogen also says in this text and other texts that we can't always tell if there's realization, if there's enlightenment, but it would be nice if somebody else could tell.
Maybe they would tell us sometime, if they're in a good mood.
"By the way, you seem so calm, so happy.
Is that that Zen thing you're doing?
I should try that."
That would be nice.
But he's not saying that.
He's not saying it's not that exactly, either, but he's not saying that Zazen is limited to that.
He's not saying that meditation is limited to being a skill that has some result.
And certainly, meditation is a complicated skill.
Ponyo Basahir was telling me that last week he gave a talk on the 40 traditional objects of meditation.
Did you know there were 40, and then a few more?
Forty and then a few more objects of meditation.
How many do you know about?
All right, your skill is not too good.
Deficient.
It's a wonderful thing to learn all these things, but then let's look at what Dogen goes on to say.
If it's not a skill, or if it's more than a skill (sometimes when he says no, he means more than), it's also the dharma gate of repose and bliss.
And so when we're practicing meditation, when we're sitting Zazen, we're not really trying to do anything.
It's a kind of resting in being itself, just being.
Dogen is suggesting that we investigate the possibility that just being, all by itself, without any extra toys or gratification or pleasures, is already joy and bliss.
So that's just something to think about the next time you're in meditation, trying to push through to the end and a little grouchy about it.
You figure it's probably good for you, and it kind of hurts.
But even in the middle of that, to see (this isn't an idea, it's experiential): can I touch into some sense of the pleasure, the joy of just being?
And so Dogen is always playing with these ideas.
On the one hand, we have to do something: our life is a mess, the world is burning, we have to do something.
On the other hand, maybe things are okay already, just as they are.
Are these two things a contradiction, or can they weave together in a certain way?
So the next part of our text, now we're in Fukanzazengi.
I'm not sure what page it will be in your books, somewhere towards the end.
Hand me a book.
So the beginning.
So we're towards the end here.
Maybe page, let me find where I'm going to start.
Yeah, okay, we're actually in the middle of the second paragraph on page 18.
In our last talk, whenever that was, it might have been a long time ago, we received some very encouraging information from Master Dogen: that we don't have to be smart.
Try to hear this.
Maybe there's enough time to be able to hear it.
At the beginning of this paragraph he says, after all the stuff he'd said before about the true nature of meditation:
*This being the case, intelligence or lack of it does not matter.
Between the dull and the sharp witted, there's no distinction.*
That's where we left off last time.
So just to practice is what he's always saying.
Just to actually really do the practice is enough.
It doesn't matter if you're going about it the best way this time, it doesn't matter if you've optimized your performance.
Just practicing is enough.
And then he says:
*If you concentrate your effort single mindedly, that in itself is negotiating the way.*
So here there does seem to be some doing.
If you concentrate your effort single mindedly, there's some sense of singularity, of not letting the mind just drift around, some sense of concentration.
But then he just the concentration, not the kind, not the result of the concentration.
We're very results oriented.
We think, "Well, what's the result of my concentration?
Then I get enlightenment, then I get meditation."
No, I said, just the concentration is already negotiating the way.
And all this writing is heavy in metaphor.
Even the way is metaphor, right?
What is the way?
Is it something we walk on?
Is it some plan we have?
Is it some way that our ancestors went that we're trying to follow?
Can we follow them?
So we don't really know what the way is.
And so you unpack these sentences, and you can do a whole talk per sentence.
He goes on to explicate this a little more, saying practice realization.
This is putting together practice and realization.
Practice realization is naturally undefiled.
"Defiled" is a reference to Buddhist terminology, that things are sort of defiled or covered up by delusion and confusion and hatred and sort of [unclear: "glaciers"].
They're saying practice and realization is naturally not that way.

So in a way, all of Mahayana Buddhism is riding on the shoulders of the earlier and older traditions of Buddhism, which are a little more specific, with forty types of meditation objects and stuff that you do.
In the earlier Buddhism, there are particular ways that you remove the defilements.
You work with different defilements in particular ways.
This is also useful to study.
We're so lucky to be Zen students in twenty-first century America.
We also have access to that material, so we can look at the earlier Buddhism and say, "Well, how did they work with the defilements?"
And we can go to [unclear: "Ponyo Basta's"] lectures and we can go to lots of other teachers and find out, well, what is he referencing?
I think we're doubly lucky, we have access to that information.
Like, for instance, Tibetan Buddhism has more of both elements in it.
It seems like the Dalai Lama talks about antidotes.
If you have a tendency towards greediness, then why not apply the antidote, which is to be generous, whether you feel like it or not, to just really be generous, to give things away.
So there are ways of working with defilements.
But then we're so lucky in Mahayana Buddhism, because we can go about that with an attitude of wholeness, an attitude of wholeness.
And I'm sure a result of doing those practices in early Buddhism is also an attitude of wholeness.
We're coming at that wholeness in a very explicit and direct way: that our life, we're already not greedy.
Our life is naturally generous.
We're just practicing the expression of that.

And there's a big difference between some sort of deep experiential recognition, like, "Oh, there's a natural, deep feeling of generosity and kindness, it's just baked into my being, or into being itself," and the other way, where it gets a little cockamamie.
So I have to practice generosity to express that.
But it's not like I'm deficient and I'm an ungenerous, greedy, nasty, stinky person and I need to fix that through external means.
Sometimes I think we think about our life and spiritual practices almost like the self is an object that can reach for objects outside the self that can poke back into the self to fix it.
And so Dogen's saying, no, no, no.
Naturally, the self is already healed, complete, an expression of love and generosity.
And then he goes on to say this is a very ordinary everyday thing.
Going forward in practice is a matter of everydayness.
And back to my character-by-character analysis, thanks to Mike Cross's fabulous website.

Other things behind the scenes here in this paragraph that aren't translated directly include characters that seem to say something about releasing the hold of the senses, which is a very traditional Buddhist idea: that we're to recognize the ways in which we're enthralled by the senses and we take the senses for reality.
One way to work with that is to really look at how incredibly interpretive sensory experience is.
And this is something we can all practice with daily.
I was just walking into our little shop, before I came here, to get my bike, and I walked by our apple tree.
We have three apple trees, and the middle apple tree, which I was closest to, was just full of apples.
It was like everywhere on there, and they're starting to turn green and red and they're starting to ripen up.
And I realized, in that moment of seeing the apples, I thought, "Oh, how beautiful."
And then what I realized is that the last time I'd walked by that apple tree, I thought, "Oh, what a pain.
I'm going to have to deal with all these apples."
It seems to be the same sensory experience, right?
Some photons bounced off these apples and came into the eye and something happened with the eye organ.
There's some kind of eye consciousness in Buddhism, or part of the brain and neurology.
Then signals get sent around and there's this whole thing that happens.
But it's really different.
It's like different apples, right?
There's the beautiful apples, and the pain apples I'm going to have to deal with, and the apples that have fallen down, and the trees that should have been pruned before.
And what's wrong with me?

I can't get around to pruning the apple trees, and I should have probably thinned the apples and had more larger apples, and that'll be easier when I go to make applesauce and get less work, and I don't have time for this.
You know what I mean?
So sometimes when you read stuff about the six senses, you think, "Oh, okay, I'm not supposed to enjoy anything."

But I think it's more like paying attention to the ways that the sensory data is manipulated and interpreted, and then our lived experience of our world is this whole other thing, generated by mind, generated by mind.
And so the way I understand abandoning the sense pleasure is to actually become more aware of the sensory experience itself.
And Then of course you also study the more obvious aspects of this, like greed for a beer or a candy bar or a smile or whatever it is.
That's a different kind of sense pleasure too, but it's not so simple as we think.
A candy bar is not a candy bar is not a candy bar either, right?
Sometimes it's a wonderful joy and sometimes it's just making you fat.
And is it the same candy bar?
It's hard to know.
So behind the scenes, there's some explication around how we actually live in the middle of these senses.
And then he goes on to say that this practice is a very universal thing, a universal human thing.
In our translation, they use the names of countries, India and China, but it turns out it's more beautiful in the characters.
I didn't write down what the characters mean, but they're like the Western heavens and the Eastern lands or something like that.
So it's more of a sense of all of heaven and earth, and it gets translated as India and China.
He probably meant both at once, because that's the other thing that's funny to think about.
We have this conceptualization of the whole globe and all these countries and things happening everywhere.

Dogen in thirteenth-century Japan knew about Japan, and he knew about China because he'd been there, but probably nobody he'd ever met had an actual lived experience of much of anywhere else, maybe the Korean peninsula, which is close by.
India is a very distant idea that none of them had been to, and very few Chinese people had even been to India because they tended to stay in China, which is a huge country.
So she means the whole world, but this practice is everywhere.
*Holding the Buddha seal, and over all prevails the character of the school, which is simply devotion to sitting, total engagement in a [unclear: "mobile"] sitting.*
So that's pretty straightforward.
Sitting practice is really central.
And he says earlier that Zazen is not just a matter of sitting down either, that the centrality of this experience is allowed to permeate all activity.
So it's not to compartmentalize Zazen too much.
It's not like some separate thing you do twenty minutes a day and then the rest of your life is some other thing.
It's all the [unclear: "piece"].

And then we're back to not worrying too much about whether we're having the right experience, because he says, and we can really let ourselves be encouraged by these things, they can be really directly speaking to us:
*Although it's said that there is many minds as there are persons, still they all negotiate the way solely in Zazen.*
So the many minds and many persons means we all get to have our own experience.
It's really complete.
It actually really is okay to have your own experience.
I've been riffing on the idea lately: is it actually really okay to be yourself?
Is that okay with you, to be yourself?
You should ask yourself that.
Maybe look in the mirror, even, maybe on a good day.
So he's saying there's a central human expression of something here, which is Zazen practice, but it's not going to look any one way.
It's going to look infinite different ways because there's infinite different kinds of people.
And this also helps us, practically speaking, in this Dharma community.
How silly it would be to judge somebody else's practice, right?
Because she doesn't look like how I suppose Zen students are supposed to look.
Well, of course she doesn't, because your idea is only your idea, emerging from your experience, and her experience is completely her experience, completely different.
But there's some common ground here, this settling into being that is settled, symbolized by Zazen.
And then there's a lot of encouragement in this last part, the last section here, to actually really do this, to not wander off in search of some perfect place and some perfect time.
I think a couple of talks ago I retold a little bit of the story of the Tibetan Rinpoche who was here, Argya Rinpoche.
I'll tell you a little bit of it again.
He was born in 1950 in Tibet, right before the Chinese invaded.

He ended up in forced education schools and forced labor on farms, and sort of in charge of monasteries, but with constant threat that any moment he might be denounced or imprisoned or killed or something like that.
And yet he still practiced.
So there are a lot of examples like that.
It's so easy for us to feel like conditions aren't quite right for me to practice, maybe later, or maybe not here, maybe if I had a better house.
So that's what he's saying.
But it's also a little bit ironic, because everybody knows when they're reading this, when he says:
*Why leave behind the seat that exists in your home and go aimlessly off to the dusty realms of other lands?*
Everybody knows that he very famously did that, right?
He very famously went to China, which was a difficult journey.
It apparently took about six weeks on the boat to get across the Sea of Japan to China, and your fate was by no means guaranteed that you were going to make it there.
So he famously did this.
And dust is always a metaphor for confused, so the confused realms of other lands.
*If you make one misstep, you go astray from the way directly before you.*
So again, our opportunity to practice is right now, right here, this next step.
And then the next part, we're talking about the Buddhist cosmology around rebirth and different types of worlds and different types of beings.
Even if we don't buy into that particular world view, which I don't even understand very well, it's still quite relevant to us, because he says:
*You've gained the pivotal opportunity of human form.*
And then he's, in a traditional Buddhist way, saying, well, you weren't reborn as an animal.
You weren't reborn as a hungry ghost.
You In those worlds, you weren't reborn in the hell realm, and in those places it's really hard to practice.

The other thing that's fun about Buddhist cosmology is that he's also saying: thank goodness you weren't reborn as a god, because the gods in Buddhism are sort of blissed out and stoned, so they don't practice.
They have really, really long lifetimes, but in Buddhism nobody's immortal.
Even the gods are eventually reborn.
They just have a really long life, but they space out for 10,000 years and then get another try.
So in our case, whether we think about those kinds of things or not, we have this brief human life, this very brief human life.
Part of what's helpful about the slow pace of Zen practice, I think, is that you practice for 10 or 20 years before the next step.
Then you think, wow.
I'm now 45, and I've been practicing since I was about 20.
How's it going with my pivotal opportunity of human form?
You can think about that, not that we have to freak out: "Oh my God, 25 years wasted, and how many more are left?"
I'm probably past the halfway point.
There are probably fewer years left than I've already lived.
And I'm younger than most of the people in the room, so sorry.
But again, back to our attitude: are we recognizing that we're naturally undefiled, or are we desperately trying to fix something that's broken?
There is some urgency here, but it can be urgency in the sense of "okay, now to practice," rather than "oh, no," which is non-practice.
So don't lose your time in vain, which is a common theme in Buddhism.
But then we also hold a big responsibility.

This is really true too, and this line has inspired me a lot: *You are maintaining the essential working of the Buddha way.* This line can come to you if you don't really feel like practicing, but actually you have a responsibility.

Not to get too heavy about it, but if everyone here and everybody else on the earth right now just said, "Oh, to hell with meditation, it just mixes me up and I'm not making any progress, and it was probably relevant in 13th century Japan, but it's not relevant now," then if we all did that, there would be no more Buddhism.
It could vanish in a generation.
Also implied in that is that the Buddha, when he was dying, supposedly forecast these huge eras of Buddhism.
The era that the Japanese Buddhists of the 13th century thought they were in was the era of decline of Buddhism.
So Dogen's probably referencing that.
Buddhism is in danger of extinction; this is urgent.
In his time, well, I guess every time is like this.
His time was really turbulent.
There was a big change going on, in the warlord dynasty.
I mentioned in a previous talk that there were large monasteries on the mountains.
So he was writing this probably in the capital somewhere around Kyoto, the sort of nominal capital.
The samurai powers were centered somewhere else, in Tokugawa.
But the imperial power was sort of there.
It was mostly symbolic and weak, mostly an exchange of symbolic support.
Anyway, the central government is weak.
There's lawlessness, there are brigands, there are warlords.
And I also mentioned that up above Kyoto there were these warrior monks.
Did I tell you about this?
The warrior monks on Mount Hiei.
The Tendai establishment on the mountain above Kyoto had an army 10,000 strong, not just a couple of guys.
So they would come in and do what they needed to do too.
It was a dangerous time.
I think the Buddhists in Tokugawa Japan really had this sense that this thing is teetering on the edge.
It could go down.
We don't know if this is going to continue.
We have the idea that things are stable, even though with climate change, Al Gore is kind of in the background.
Al's kind of back there somewhere, and for some of us he's more present than others, I think.
With all that's going on, we have a sense maybe of, wow, we're teetering on the edge too.
But later.
We're stable for now.
I think it didn't feel stable even for now in the 1220s and 1230s in Japan.
It felt like, wow, what's going to happen?
So they had to maintain the essential working of the Buddha way.

*And who would take wasteful delight in the spark from a Flintstone?* So if there is a spark, light, awakening, some sense of illumination, some sense of awakening, we're not just going to say "whoop-de-doo."
We're really going to treasure that: "Okay, it's important.
We have to keep practicing." [unclear: "before feeling the Buddha way in that system"] Light is here and we have to maintain that light.
And this next part is a quote from the Diamond Sutra:
*Besides, form and substance are like the dew on the grass, destiny like a dart of lightning, emptied an instant, vanished in a flash.*
So this is, of course, impermanence.
One of Japanese culture's most highly refined sensibilities, I think, is the appreciation for impermanence, for things that are beautiful because they're gone.
Everything's so temporary in our whole life, like dew on the grass.
It's good to notice the dew, to really look at the dew sometime.
It's not there very long.
Like a dart of lightning.
*Just so please, honored followers of Zen, long accustomed to groping for the elephant, do not be suspicious of the true dragon.*
So this is actually just what you think, as a reference to the famous ancient Indian story of the blind men and the elephant, which is, I think, from at least 1000 or maybe 2000 BC.
It's an old story, and we know it still today.
Isn't that amazing?
Human culture.
Do you know the story of the blind men and the elephant?
There are blind men, and they come up to an elephant, but each comes to a different part, right?
So this is back to perception.
We are all the blind men and the elephant.
That's how we interact with the world, right?
One person gets to the foot and says, "Oh, this thing called an elephant is like a pillar."
Another person gets to the trunk and says, "No, it's like an icicle or a rock," or I don't know how it's written exactly, but you get the idea.
Someone gets the tail and says, "No, no, it's really floppy and fuzzy and it's like a rope."
What are you talking about?
They probably argued, pretty stupidly.
And then the dragon symbolizes enlightenment.
We're used to groping for the elephant, so we don't recognize the true dragon, which is right there, right in front of us, right in us.
We are the true dragon.
So again, there's a kind of encouragement to experientially enter our life with contentment, with joy, with completion.
Devote your energies in a way that directly indicates the absolute.
So let our actions and words and deeds be grounded in Dharma.
This is a reference to the precepts.
When we're goofing off and indulging ourselves and gossiping and so on, that's indicating the relative.
The relative is the world of differentiation and things: one thing is better than another, good, bad, dark and light.
The absolute is the world of nirvana, of enlightenment.
So let our energies indicate the absolute, and that's actually a beautiful way of thinking about it.
You can't really talk about the absolute, right, because it's non-differentiated, non-conceptual, the flow of experience.
But sometimes you meet somebody who's having a nice day and is feeling really grounded, and you know what I mean?
Or even you yourself, or a sunset, or a bird, or a mountain, or mountains and rivers hiking retreat, or the rain.
Sometimes you get that feeling like, wow, there's something here, something deep here.
Maybe that's what he means: this is indicating the absolute.
And he's saying that our behavior can do this or not do this.
We can indicate the absolute, or stir up the relative.
Stir up the relative.
So there's a lot here, a lot of encouragement from a lot of different angles.
*Gain accord with the enlightenment of the Buddhas.
Succeed to the legitimate lineage of the ancestors' samadhi.* Samadhi is also technical Buddhist jargon for deep meditation states.
It has a lot of shades of meaning, more than we want to go into right now.
But again, this is the idea of lineage he brought up in the beginning.
The text has three sections.
There's an introductory section, which brought up for the first time this sense of completion and perfection of our life, and brought up lineage as an expression of that.
There's a middle section, which is nuts and bolts: how to sit, how to stand, what to eat.
And then there's this final section, which circles back to encouragement and poetry about what this process is.
In it he also brings up lineage, as he did earlier; whenever he mentions Buddhas, he's talking about lineage.
I think this was really true for Dogen in a felt way.
We think of lineage as an abstraction, but I really feel, and Jeff and I have talked a lot about how the Native community feels this in a felt way a little more than we do.
Maybe we are just appreciating this more and more: that we're only here because of the ones who came before, and we can really feel them, and the ones who come after us are there too.
So, lineage, like line, right?
We're always in this line in a certain position, and we need to hold up our place or the whole thing collapses.
I've been studying another Dogen text, preparing.
We're going to do a whole weekend on Dogen, so if this isn't enough, you can come for a whole weekend on October 15th and 16th.
In that text I've been learning a little more about where he got some of the stories and metaphors and images.
Some of them are from his teacher, but quite a few of them are from another ancestor named Hongzhi, who was the abbot of the same monastery a hundred years before.
I was thinking about it, and I bet it really meant a lot to Dogen that he was practicing in Hongzhi's monastery.
We have a Library of Congress, a way of looking at knowledge and ranking knowledge: this is good, this is bad, this is a world treasure, and this is like TV.
But I think he wasn't evaluating things in quite that way.
There's a sense of: this was spoken by my ancestor, so I need to understand and appreciate it, because this is my ancestor.
Hongzhi was in our lineage and also in the same physical place.
And I think Zen is more place-based than we recognize.
We think of Zen as an abstract philosophy, something beyond thinking.
I was thinking about that with Bob's maniac gardening work this last weekend.
Not just Bob; many of us came together over the weekend.
It's a little hard to see in the dark, so come back, you must come back during the day if you haven't already, and look at the back parking lot, because it is no longer a parking lot.
It is now a stream and a mountain range.
No, I'm not kidding, it really is.
And so we were establishing Taking care of our place, in our funny way: our case involved backhoes and landscaping businesses and stuff, but also our intention and our love for the place.
Dogen, I think, had a real sense of place, both when he was in China and when he was in Japan, practicing inside and outside Kyoto.
Then he established his own place in the mountains, starting in the mountains.
So let's see if we can finish, and then I have a few textual notes.
I have to correct myself from an earlier lecture.
"Gain accord with the enlightenment of the Buddhas."
I don't know if I looked up this one so much, but "gain accord" doesn't really roll off the tongue.
It's not really the way we speak, and sometimes awkward English is because it's just hard to translate the Chinese characters he was using.
I'll have to look that up later.
But maybe we could say "be in harmony with," "be in touch with," or maybe actually "touch."
The word that we use for our formal multi-day meditation retreat, sesshin, actually means to touch the heart, to touch the mind.
So maybe it means something like that.
"Gain accord" kind of sounds like "throw me a line, Buddha," or I don't know what.
So: be in harmony with the enlightenment of the Buddhas, succeed to the legitimate lineage of the ancestors, samadhi.
Take our place, constantly perform in such a manner.
Constancy is a theme you might have noticed, steadiness in practice.
The thing about it is, it's hard to be steady if we think meditation is a skill that we're trying to get better at.
That actually makes it quite a bit harder to be steady, because then we have judgment, we have evaluation, we have progress or lack of progress, we have skipping a day.
Not skipping a day.
But if zazen is resting in something, resting in being, then it's more possible to be constant and lifelong about it, because whatever effort we make is sufficient.
Whatever we do is just absolutely okay, it's just fine.
We make effort and that effort is enough.
"Concentrate your effort single-mindedly": that's enough.
It's not saying reach a level.
Why in concentration?
In fact, back to meditation objects, he hardly talks about meditation objects whatsoever.
He just says show up and make effort.
That's the other thing that's strange about Zen: there are actually very few texts about how to actually do meditation.
In earlier Buddhism there were lots of texts about how to actually do it, do meditation, do Buddhism.
But Zen texts, and Mahayana texts in general, are more of an encouragement to feel the wholeness of being, and from there take a step.
*If you do all this, you are assured of being a person such as they.* That sounds like he's sort of reversing himself, like, oh, that sounds like cause and effect.
Like, okay, now you're saying if I do this I get to be a person such as they.
So maybe he means that, but maybe he also means you already were a person such as they.
*Your treasure store will open of itself, and you will use it at will.* So "treasure store" maybe means something like your deepest heart, your biggest self.
That sense we have of separation and being a little bit closed can open, and we can all experience this.
I'm sure most all of us have experienced this at different times in our life, on meditation retreat or other times.
Sometimes the heart just opens, you know what I mean?
There's no obvious cause and effect.
You weren't really nice for eleven days in a row and then it just happens.
The treasure store opens of itself, and so "of itself" is important.
You're not going to make the treasure store open, like prying the gates open.
Sometimes self-improvement, sort of misunderstood, can have that quality.
